units.translation: 207-09a. And from Phocis: the Phocians were named after Phocus, son of Aeacus. They trace Iphitus' lineage to Naubolus and Perineice, daughter of Hippomachus. Pytho is a city of Phocis, where the oracle is, so called from inquiring of the oracles (πυνθάνεσθαι) or from the dragon having rotted (σεσῆφθαι) there.

b. 〈ξεῖνος:〉 He was a friend of Jason. Lg

c. Zetes and Calais: they say that these sailed with the Argonauts from different places. For some say from Thrace, as Apollonius; Herodorus (31 FGrH 46 J.) from Daulis; Duris (76 FGrH 86 J.) from the Hyperboreans. Antimachus (fr. 7 B. II 290) also lists them. Phanodicus in the first book of his Deliaca (fr. 1 M. IV 473) says that they came from the Hyperboreans for the voyage. Simonides (fr. 3 B. III 382) says that Orithyia was snatched from Brilessus and carried to the Sarpedonian rock of Thrace; for there is also one of the same name in Cilicia, as Callisthenes (124 FGrH 39 J.) says. Stesichorus in the Geryoneis (fr. 10 B. III 210) says that there is also a certain island in the Atlantic sea called Sarpedonia. Concerning the Thracian Sarpedonian rock, that it is near Mount Haemus, Pherecydes (3 FGrH 145 J.) says, when relating the abduction of Orithyia. Choerilus (fr. 5 Kink.) says that she was snatched while gathering flowers by the springs of Cephisus. Heragoras in his Megarica (fr. 4 M. IV 427) says that the one who snatched Orithyia was Boreas, son of Strymon, not the wind. Orithyia was the daughter of Erechtheus, whom Boreas snatched from Attica and brought to Thrace, and there he lay with her and fathered Zetes and Calais, as Simonides says in the Naumachia (see above). 〈...〉 Phineus first married Cleopatra, daughter of Orithyia, and afterwards Idaea, daughter of Dardanus, who, being hostile to the stepchildren, I mean the sons of Cleopatra, tried to blind them. But they, because their father blinded them after their stepmother slandered them to him.
